progression.startsWith: Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol share the formula C three H eight O, so in a mass spectrum both molecular ions sit at 60. Both are alcohols, so both infrared spectra show the broad O H band. So how do you tell them apart? Run a carbon-13 NMR spectrum. One gives three peaks, and the other gives two. By the end of this video, you'll know which is which, and why.
progression.stopsAfter: explaining resonance and shielding in a sentence each; reading the ppm scale; counting carbon environments with symmetry; explaining single lines and why heights aren't counts; assigning shifts from the data sheet; choosing between candidates with the count, shifts and formula.

teaching.task: Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol share a formula, a molecular ion and an O–H band. How can carbon-13 NMR tell them apart at a glance?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) a formula, a molecular ion and an O–H band can match; carbon-13 NMR counts something else (1); (2) ¹³C and ¹H nuclei act as tiny magnets; in a strong field they line up with or against it; the right radio frequency flips them: resonance (2); (3) electrons shield a nucleus; oxygen pulls electron density away, so the carbon is deshielded and needs a slightly higher frequency (3); (4) that position is the chemical shift, in ppm, read right to left from TMS at zero; deshielded means further left; carbon-13 runs to about 220 (4); (5) carbons in identical surroundings share an environment and a peak; ethanol: two (5); (6) symmetry: carbons that swap share a peak; propan-1-ol three, propan-2-ol two (6); (7) the swap test on butan-2-one and pentan-3-one; atoms are not environments (7); (8) each environment is one line, and heights aren't counts, with the causes (8); (9) shifts read off the data sheet: ethyl ethanoate (9); (10) ranges overlap; the formula and the other peaks settle it (10); memory aid (11); attempts (12 to 15); decision rule and handoff (16); key notes (17).
teaching.conversationalApproach: Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol share the formula C three H eight O, so in a mass spectrum both molecular ions sit at 60. NMR stands for nuclear magnetic resonance. Here's the useful part. That position is the chemical shift, measured in parts per million, or ppm. So what makes two carbons give the same peak? They need identical surroundings, which chemists call the same environment. Back to the propanols. Try the swap test on two ketones. You might expect a taller peak to mean more carbons. Where a peak sits tells you what kind of carbon it is. The ranges overlap, so one shift can fit more than one kind of carbon. Two lines to keep. Your turn. It's 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Last one. It's methyl ethanoate. So, with a carbon-13 spectrum, count the peaks to count the carbon environments, and use symmetry to merge carbons that swap.
teaching.openingDecision: Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol share the formula C three H eight O, so in a mass spectrum both molecular ions sit at 60. Both are alcohols, so both infrared spectra show the broad O H band. So how do you tell them apart? Run a carbon-13 NMR spectrum. One gives three peaks, and the other gives two. By the end of this video, you'll know which is which, and why.
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "The four alcohols below all have the molecular formula C₄H₁₀O: butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol. One of them gives a ¹³C NMR spectrum with two peaks, at 69 ppm and 31 ppm. Identify the alcohol, and explain the number of peaks and their chemical shifts." Answer: 2-methylpropan-2-ol; its three CH₃ carbons swap places around the central carbon (one environment, 31 ppm, alkyl); the central carbon carries the OH (C–O range 50 to 90, 69 ppm); butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol give four peaks, 2-methylpropan-1-ol three. Crossed mistake: "four carbons, so four peaks". (A2) "A compound with molecular formula C₃H₆O₂ is either propanoic acid or methyl ethanoate. Its ¹³C NMR spectrum shows three peaks, at 171 ppm, 52 ppm and 21 ppm. Identify the compound. Justify your answer using the ¹³C NMR chemical shift data on the data sheet." Answer: methyl ethanoate; 171 is a C=O carbon, but 160 to 185 covers both acids and esters, so it can't decide; 52 lies in the C–O range (50 to 90), a carbon singly bonded to oxygen (the ester's OCH₃); propanoic acid has no peak in that range (about 181, 28 and 9). Crossed mistake: "171 ppm, so it's an acid".

design.visualSystem: the NMR machine and the sample tube as painted plates listed by filename, never stretched; spectra are coded diagrams only (the new NmrSpectrum component), with realistic shifts for the named compounds, never AI images; molecules come from the coded molecule kit (src/explainer/lessons/chem-m7-c01/molecules.tsx), with each carbon environment ringed in the same colour as its peak; nuclear magnets, field lines and electron clouds coded as abstract diagrams; no people, hands or faces (the tube drops into the magnet as coded motion); at most about three bright text items, earlier lines dim; one reasoning stage at a time; "Pause here to answer." then a 10 s countdown with the full worded question kept on screen; no givens card, givens underlined in the feedback as they are used; brief feedback (answer, key reason, one crossed mistake, about 15 to 30 s); original HSC-style questions only; Australian spelling; no em dashes; conversational narration; no absolute claims ("usually", "points to", "fits").
